claims.claim: (a-AIME) AIME accuracy base vs effm1s30: low 0.475 -> 0.633 (paired diff +0.158, 95% CI excludes 0), medium 0.842 -> 0.875, high 0.783 -> 0.800
claims.your_numbers: low 0.475 -> 0.633, paired diff +0.158, question-bootstrap CI [+0.083, +0.242] (B=10000, seed 0); two-level bootstrap (questions, then samples within) [+0.058, +0.267]; sign-flip p<1e-4; 15 questions up, 1 down, 14 tied. medium 0.842 -> 0.875, diff +0.033 [-0.050, +0.117]. high 0.783 -> 0.800, diff +0.017 [-0.042, +0.075].

The low gain matches what base's own accuracy-vs-length curve predicts for the trained model's longer low-effort CoT (see simplest_wrong_explanation): taking base's low-to-medium slope per ln-token (0.268) at trained low's mean CoT of 2376 tokens predicts 0.615 pooled and 0.634 per question; observed is 0.633.

claims.claim: (a-DAPO) DAPO held-out accuracy: low 0.837 -> 0.873, medium 0.947 -> 0.980 (CI excludes 0), high 0.953 -> 0.933
claims.comment: Reproduces. The medium CI excludes 0 only narrowly: with the two-level bootstrap the lower bound is +0.003, on a set at ceiling (0.95-0.98). claims.claim: (b) The high-minus-low accuracy gap shrinks: AIME +0.308 -> +0.167 (change CI excludes 0), DAPO +0.117 -> +0.060
claims.your_numbers: AIME: base gap +0.308 [+0.200, +0.425], effm1 gap +0.167 [+0.058, +0.283]; change -0.142, question-bootstrap CI [-0.242, -0.050], two-level CI [-0.267, -0.017], sign-flip p=0.009. Breaking the change into parts: on AIME the low-effort difference is +0.158 and the high-effort difference is +0.017; on DAPO they are +0.037 and -0.020. claims.comment: The numbers and the AIME CI reproduce. Two caveats. First, the shrinking gap is the same fact as claim (a)'s low-effort gain, restated: on AIME the high-effort accuracy did not move, and the gap closes because low effort became more accurate. Second, on DAPO about half the change comes from extra high-effort truncations. The DAPO change is significant only under the question-level bootstrap; the two-level CI includes 0, and it does not survive any truncation correction (see d).

claims.claim: (c-mean) Mean CoT trained/base on matched questions: AIME 1.69 / 1.51 / 1.04, DAPO 1.50 / 1.32 / 1.04 (low/medium/high)
claims.comment: Reproduces, computed as the ratio of question-mean CoT means. At high effort the ratio of about 1.0 is partly compressed by the 32k cap, because 20% of AIME high samples are pinned at about 32k tokens. Trained low and medium got longer even though the reward penalizes ln(CoT).

claims.your_numbers: AIME: base medians low 1076 / high 12446 = 11.57x, effm1 1908 / 12904 = 6.76x; paired change -4.81, CI [-7.79, -1.22]. claims.comment: Reproduces, as the median over all samples at high divided by the median over all samples at low. Almost all of the compression comes from low getting longer: the low median grew 1.77x on AIME, while the high median grew only 1.04x.

claims.claim: (d) Truncations at the 32k cap (base AIME high 20%, effm1 19.2%): how much do they shape the high-effort accuracy and the gap? Recompute the gap on finished samples, and with truncated high samples scored using the same model's medium result
claims.your_numbers: Truncation rates: AIME high, base 24/120 = 20.0% across 8 questions and effm1 23/120 = 19.2% across 8 questions. DAPO high, base 11/300 (3.7%) and effm1 17/300 (5.7%). All 79 truncated rows have an empty response and are scored 0. AIME high accuracy on finished samples is 0.979 (base) and 0.990 (effm1), so truncation accounts for the entire high < medium inversion. Finished samples only, per question (4 AIME questions with no finished samples dropped, n=26): AIME gap base +0.429, effm1 +0.266, change -0.163 [-0.266, -0.067]; pooled over samples, base +0.504 and effm1 +0.356. DAPO (n=144): +0.139 -> +0.097, change -0.042 [-0.090, +0.007]. Truncated high samples set to the same model's question-mean medium accuracy: AIME high base 0.850, effm1 0.898; gap +0.375 -> +0.265, change -0.110 [-0.217, -0.006], sign-flip p=0.058. Using the medium sample with the same sample_idx instead gives -0.125 [-0.233, -0.017], p=0.053. DAPO, medium-imputed: high base 0.980, effm1 0.985; gap +0.143 -> +0.112, change -0.032 [-0.083, +0.020]. Upper bound with truncated samples counted correct: AIME change -0.150 [-0.233, -0.067]; DAPO -0.037 [-0.087, +0.013]. The high-effort difference (effm1 - base) is near 0 under every variant: AIME +0.008 to +0.048, DAPO -0.003 to +0.005.
claims.comment: Truncation sets the absolute high-effort accuracy: without it, both models score about 0.98-0.99 on AIME high instead of about 0.79, and the gap is roughly 0.1-0.2 larger. It does not create the AIME gap shrinkage, which survives every variant. Under medium imputation, though, the change weakens to -0.110 and is borderline (bootstrap CI barely excludes 0, sign-flip p about 0.055). On DAPO, the gap shrinkage and the -0.020 high-effort deficit both disappear once truncation is handled, so they are truncation artifacts. The truncations fall on the same hard AIME questions (13, 14, 15, 20, 28, 30, 9) for both models. AIME 14 and 15 are never solved at any effort and all their high samples hit the cap.

data_problems:
The data passes the integrity checks. rows.jsonl has 2520 rows, the complete grid: 2 models x (30 AIME x 4 + 150 DAPO x 2) x 3 efforts. There are no duplicate keys (model, set, dataset, qid, effort, sample_idx) and no repeated reasoning or response texts. The qid sets match the golds exactly: 30 MathArena/aime_2025 problems loaded via math_data.load_aime25(), and the 150 qids of rl/data/math_heldout.jsonl. Regrading every response with math_data.parse_answer against the gold reproduces the stored `correct` field on all 2520 rows. Truncated rows (finish=length, 79 rows) total 31955-31998 re-encoded tokens, consistent with the 32,000-token cap. Each has an empty response and is scored wrong. Finished rows reach at most 31262 tokens.

Issues found:
(1) Gold/format ambiguity on DAPO qid 18c14a08. The problem asks for 'the largest power of 5 that divides x_2014^2+1' and the gold is 2014 (the exponent). Both models mostly answer 'ANSWER: 5^{2014}', which parse_answer rejects as a power, so 9 semantically correct samples (4 base, 5 effm1) are scored wrong. Regrading them moves DAPO cells by at most +0.007 and changes no conclusion. On this question 10 of 12 finished parses are None, so the build_math_pool suspect-gold filter, which requires a single non-None consensus, missed it.
(2) Held-out DAPO qid 3fbfa356 is a near-duplicate of training-pool qid 897af174: the same Chinese log problem with the same answer, 3, differing only in wording and whitespace. load_dapo dedups by exact prompt text only. check_overlap flags this as the only pool/held-out pair, so 1 of 150 held-out problems is effectively a training item. check_overlap finds no AIME overlap with the pool or the held-out set.
(3) Two finished responses have no ANSWER line. Two AIME questions (14, 15) are never solved by either model at any effort, and all their high-effort samples are truncated.
(4) The held-out DAPO problems were filtered on base's earlier low/medium performance (never-solved and suspect-gold problems dropped). The set is therefore near ceiling (0.95-0.98 at medium/high), which limits headroom and makes the DAPO medium CI fragile: its two-level-bootstrap lower bound is +0.003.
(5) summary.md does not report the paired-difference CIs or the gap-change CI cited in the claims. I computed them myself (question-level bootstrap, B=10000, seed 0; two-level bootstrap, B=3000, seed 7; sign-flip permutation). They agree with the claims.

simplest_wrong_explanation: The effort-trained model did not become better at calibrating effort or at reasoning efficiently at low effort. Its 'low' mode simply thinks about 1.7x longer and moves along base's own accuracy-vs-length curve. Base's low-to-medium accuracy slope per ln-token, applied to the trained model's mean low-effort CoT length, predicts trained low accuracy almost exactly. On AIME it predicts 0.615 pooled and 0.634 per-question interpolated, against 0.633 observed. On DAPO it predicts 0.881 and 0.880, against 0.873 observed. The shrinking high-minus-low accuracy gap and the falling high/low CoT ratio restate this same fact: low got longer and more accurate while high-effort accuracy and length stayed put (AIME high diff +0.017, CoT ratio 1.04). On DAPO, the remaining part of the gap shrinkage, and effm1's lower high-effort accuracy, come from effm1 hitting the 32k cap more often (17 vs 11 truncations). Both vanish when truncated samples are dropped or imputed from medium. The AIME high-below-medium inversion for both models is also purely a truncation artifact: high-effort accuracy on finished samples is 0.98-0.99.

claims.claim: (e-1) AIME, low effort: CoTs grew 2.32x on 'hard' problems (base medium accuracy < 1, n=6) vs 1.50x on 'easy' problems (n=24), measured as ratio of means trained/base.
claims.your_numbers: Hard 2.320 (n=6), easy 1.500 (n=24). Difference +0.82. Stratified problem bootstrap 95% CI [+0.39, +1.37]. Two-level bootstrap (problems, then samples) [+0.27, +1.52]. Relabel permutation p=0.022. Median per-problem ratio: hard 2.30, easy 1.42, Mann-Whitney p=0.001. Leave-one-out hard ratio ranges 2.20 to 2.47. Dropping the top 1/2/3 hard problems by absolute growth gives 2.47/2.29/2.21. All 6 hard per-problem ratios (1.71 to 3.58) are above the easy median; 8.3% of easy problems exceed the hard median. Other difficulty definitions: base high acc<1 (n=9) 2.39 vs 1.30, CI [+0.61, +1.71]; base low acc<1 (n=22) 1.77 vs 1.30, CI [+0.13, +0.85], perm p=0.17; base medium CoT top 20% 2.56 vs 1.43; trained medium acc<1 2.31 vs 1.44. Continuous: Spearman(log per-problem ratio, 1 - base medium acc) +0.58 (p=0.001), with pooled base accuracy +0.62, with base low CoT length -0.03. So short base-low CoTs are not what grows.
claims.comment: The effect is robust and no single problem drives it. The extra length buys almost no accuracy on these 6 problems: trained-low accuracy 0.083 vs base-low 0.000. The hard set is mostly problems neither model solves at low effort.

claims.claim: (e-2) DAPO held-out, low effort: 2.14x on hard (n=13) vs 1.41x on easy (n=137).
claims.your_numbers: Hard 2.140 (n=13), easy 1.411 (n=137). Difference +0.73. Stratified bootstrap CI [+0.34, +1.27]; two-level [+0.22, +1.43]; permutation p=0.005. Leave-one-out 2.03 to 2.21. claims.claim: (e-3) Spearman(length, base difficulty) at low rose from 0.38 to 0.65 (AIME) and from 0.17 to 0.25 (DAPO).

On the 18 AIME problems where base medium beats base low: 0.35 to 0.60 vs 0.96.

claims.claim: (f-2) Where trained-low is right and base-low wrong, is the gain from longer genuine reasoning, from fewer guesses/give-ups, or something else? (6 CoTs read)
claims.your_numbers: Six trained-low CoTs read against all base-low samples on the same problems. (1) aime25-20 (gold 336), trained s0, 4355 tokens: a full coordinate computation of the arcs ('Arc HJ ... difference =23.6°. Probably exactly 24°'). Three of the four base-low samples are explicit give-ups: 'Given time, guess answer maybe 180', 'Running out time. Guess ... try 360', 'Time low ... I'll guess'. (2) 38a143e3 (gold 12), 1172 tokens: complete inclusion-exclusion with an exclusivity argument. Both base-low samples guess: 'Given time low, I'll guess answer 44', 'I'll make a guess 56'. (3) d262fdb5 (gold 5), 2180 tokens: rules out k=2,3,4 by residues mod 9 and 7, then gives a witness, 5+63*3+49=243=3^5. Base-low s0 proves k≠2, then jumps: 'Likely possible. So minimal k=3'; s1: 'Probably answer is k=2'. (4) aime25-23 (gold 610), s1: the same characterization base reached, plus the N<25 edge case ('overcounts those small N (1-24) ... failures = 400 -10 = 390'). The base-low samples got the characterization right but answered 600, 600, 800, 400 because they missed the edge case or inverted it. (5) 903f8d02 (gold 338): same method as base, plus a domain check ('a=b=-n^2 yields x = y =0, invalid'). Both base-low samples answer 340. (6) 7ffb2ec0 (gold 9): derives x1^8=8 correctly, then finds the result irrational and guesses: 'Given weirdness, I'll answer with m+n = 8+1 =9'. Correct by luck. Base-low: 40 and 60 token guesses. Regex for guess/time markers at low effort: AIME 25.8% to 20.0% of samples, DAPO 11.3% to 8.0%. Decomposition: AIME +0.027 of the +0.158 gain from fewer marker samples and +0.131 from higher accuracy within strata (unmarked samples 0.60 to 0.75); DAPO +0.020 and +0.016.
claims.comment: Both effects appear. In 3 of 6 cases base-low gives up explicitly and trained-low does the work. In the other 3, base-low reasons correctly but stops early: it skips an edge case or domain check, or asserts an unproven step. Trained-low completes the verification. One of the 6 trained wins is partly a lucky guess. Overall the gain comes more from more complete reasoning on problems base attempts than from eliminating guesses. The guess-marker regex is crude and was not validated by hand beyond these reads.

claims.claim: (g) effm1s30's eval CoTs show the token-level glitches seen in training (stray foreign-script tokens, glued words like 'simultaneouslyUser', odd substitutions like 'jquery?') more than base's, as a rate per million words.
claims.your_numbers: The same detectors were run on all 1260 CoTs per model (3.28M base words, 3.88M trained words, whitespace tokens). Foreign-script runs (non-Latin/Greek scripts not in the problem; CJK ignored on the 27 Chinese problems): base 0; trained 3, all at high effort ('But we должно also consider N less than 25', 'point k (к)', '|T \\атели? Actually'), 1.23/M at high, 0.77/M overall, exact p=0.25. Hand-labelled misspellings from an automatic one-edit-from-a-common-word detector (wordfreq zipf>=3.5, token unknown, not in the problem, in <=2 CoTs): base 9 (8 high, 1 medium) = 3.45/M at high; trained 17 (all high; e.g. occcurs, overllap, strengten, mappingu, nepot) = 6.99/M; rate ratio 2.02 [0.83, 5.42], p=0.11. Unlabelled automatic near-misses: 10.28 vs 7.34/M at high, ratio 1.40, p=0.36. Role-word glue (xxxUser/Assistant): 0 in both. camelCase hits are all legitimate variable names in both models. Glued lowercase words: trained 2 ('thesecos', 'thevalue'), base 1 ('aresome', counted among base typos). A curated list of out-of-place tech words, excluding 'ChatGPT', which both models use for self-reference: base 1 ('meltdown'), trained 0 glitches. Foreign + typo + glue at high: trained 22 (9.05/M) vs base 8 (3.45/M), ratio 2.62 [1.12, 6.80], p=0.017. All levels: 5.67 vs 2.74/M, p=0.071. Low effort: 0 glitches for both models (trained low 340k words). Medium: base 1, trained 0. Rare real words (zipf<2, in one CoT only): 54.3 vs 44.5/M, ratio 1.22, p=0.063; at high 1.12, p=0.34. Both lists are mostly legitimate math vocabulary, with occasional odd words in both models (base: 'exosphere', 'attenders'; trained: 'elementos', 'reste', 'grees', 'literarily'). The 21 trained glitch CoTs span 13 problems; the 9 base ones span 8.
claims.comment: There is a weak sign, confined to high effort: about 2-2.6x base's rate and a qualitatively new class (Cyrillic fragments, 3 vs 0). Each category alone is not significant. Only the post hoc combined count reaches p≈0.02, and I made the typo labels after seeing which model each token came from. Low and medium are clean. No 'jquery'-style or role-glued tokens appear in this eval. The training spot-check's '53-94 per M words' method was not preserved, so these rates are not comparable to it.

simplest_wrong_explanation:
For the headline Spearman rise (0.38 to 0.65, 0.17 to 0.25), the simplest wrong explanation is the right one. Ordinal ranks with ties broken by file order, which is completion order and so correlates with CoT length, produce most of the reported correlation for both models. The real tie-aware values are 0.03 to 0.35 and 0.14 to 0.29.

For the hard-vs-easy CoT ratio, the obvious artifacts do not explain it: no single outlier problem carries it (LOO and medians agree), short base-low CoTs do not inflate the ratio (Spearman with base-low length ≈0), and an alternative model's difficulty or base-high difficulty gives the same result. The remaining caveat is magnitude. The DAPO 2.14x comes from a noisy 2-sample difficulty split; with independent or pooled difficulty the gap shrinks to about 1.6-1.85x vs 1.34x.

For (f), the simplest wrong reading would be 'trained low = base medium' or 'it just stops guessing'. Neither holds: trained low closes about 40% of the gap, and most of the AIME gain comes from more complete reasoning (edge cases, domain checks, finishing the case analysis) on attempts base-low also makes, with fewer give-ups as a smaller part.

For (g), the most likely wrong explanation is post hoc hand labelling plus multiple comparisons. Only the combined high-effort count is significant (p≈0.02), and the 3 vs 0 Cyrillic difference alone is p=0.25.
